title: Approve chapter 3 of The Last Signal

result.title: The Wasteland's Rules
result.content_text:
The overpass had been a highway once. Now it was a toll road.

Mara saw the barricade from two hundred yards out, a pair of rusted pickup trucks angled nose-to-nose across the cracked asphalt, their beds loaded with sandbags that had leaked half their fill onto the road. Behind the trucks, three figures stood in the particular way of people who were used to waiting and had decided to make waiting look like power. One of them held a rifle across her chest. Not aimed. Just present.

"Checkpoint," Tomás said, which was unnecessary.

"I see it."

"We go around, it adds four hours. There's no clean route through the gully, I checked the map last night."

Mara was already calculating. The receiver was strapped to her pack, wrapped in a cut-up wool blanket that smelled of the woman she'd traded two batteries to get it from, three settlements back. It wasn't hidden. Hiding it would be worse than showing it.

"We go through," she said.

They walked toward the barricade at the pace of people with nothing to hide, which was the pace of people who had learned that running looked like guilt and stillness looked like arrogance. The middle distance was the right speed.

The woman with the rifle stepped forward when they were twenty feet out. She was Mara's age, maybe a few years older, with a jaw like a fence post and eyes that moved in short, professional sweeps, pack, hands, face, pack again. Her jacket was military surplus, the kind that had been repaired so many times the original fabric was a minority of what remained. A hand-stitched patch on the left shoulder read RIDGEWAY COMPACT in letters that had been done carefully, by someone who cared.

"Road's closed to through traffic," the woman said.

"We're not traffic," Tomás said. "We're two people on foot."

"Road's closed to through people."

Mara let Tomás handle the next thirty seconds. He was better at this, he had the kind of face that looked like it had already heard every possible answer and wasn't surprised by any of them. He asked about the toll, which was the right question because it acknowledged the real structure of the conversation without pretending they were having a different one.

The toll was two tins of food per person, or equivalent trade.

They paid it. Mara handed over a tin of black beans and a stub of candle she'd been carrying as backup. Tomás gave two tins without comment.

The woman, one of the others called her Fen, and the name fit her like the jacket fit her: functional, worn in, pocketed the tins and then looked at Mara's pack again. At the shape of the receiver under the blanket.

"What's that."

Not a question. Mara had heard that tone before. It was the tone of someone who already knew the answer and was giving you the chance to tell the truth about it.

"Radio receiver," Mara said. "Passive. It doesn't transmit."

"Show me."

Mara unslung her pack and unwrapped the receiver on the hood of the nearest truck, which was still warm from the morning sun. The casing was grey plastic, cracked along one edge and repaired with electrical tape that had gone brittle in the cold. The dial face was scratched. The speaker grille had a dent in it from a fall she'd taken eighteen months ago in a ditch outside Harmon. It was the ugliest piece of equipment she owned and she had carried it for four years.

Fen picked it up and turned it over in her hands with the careful attention of someone who didn't know what they were looking at but understood that not knowing was a disadvantage.

"What frequencies?"

"Shortwave. HF band. I scan atmospheric static, mostly."

"Mostly."

"Entirely," Mara said, which was close enough to true.

Fen set the receiver down and looked at her. "Ridgeway Compact ordinance. Any equipment capable of receiving or transmitting signal across district boundaries requires a license from the council. You have a license?"

"I didn't know Ridgeway had a district."

"It does now."

Tomás said, very carefully, "How much is a license?"

"Council issues them in Ridgeway proper. We're three days that direction." Fen pointed east, away from everything they needed. "You want to go apply, be our guests."

Mara looked at the receiver. She looked at Fen. She said, "That's not a licensing ordinance. That's a confiscation."

Something shifted in Fen's expression, not guilt, not embarrassment, but the faint acknowledgment of a person who has been named accurately and doesn't particularly care. "Equipment stays here until you produce a license or until you come back through from Ridgeway with one. It'll be logged and held." She nodded at the steel cage bolted to the inside of the guardrail, a livestock crate, by the look of it, retrofitted with a padlock that was newer than anything else on the overpass. Inside it, Mara could see a solar lantern, a hand-crank torch, and what looked like a CB radio with its antenna snapped off.

"That's a graveyard," Mara said.

"That's a secure holding facility."

"You're never going to give any of it back."

Fen picked up the receiver and walked toward the cage. "You're welcome to wait here while we send a runner to Ridgeway and ask the council to send someone out with the paperwork. Probably two weeks."

Mara took two steps after her. The man with the rifle, she hadn't been watching him closely enough, which was a mistake, moved to intercept, not blocking her, just repositioning, the way a chess piece repositions to change the geometry of the board.

She stopped.

She watched Fen set the receiver inside the cage, watched the padlock snap shut, watched the receiver sit there among the other dead things with its cracked casing and its four years of scratches.

Eleven days. She had eleven days from the moment the countdown in the third transmission began, and she didn't know when that was yet because she hadn't finished decoding the second layer, and she couldn't decode the second layer without the receiver, and the receiver was in a cage on an overpass in a district that hadn't existed six months ago.

"The antenna," she said. "Can I at least keep the antenna?"

Fen looked at her for a moment. Then she unlocked the cage, removed the telescoping antenna from the receiver's input port, and handed it to Mara without a word.

It was a gesture that could have been contempt or could have been something almost like pity. Mara took the antenna and didn't try to decide which it was.

They walked through the checkpoint and down the far side of the overpass, and Tomás didn't say anything until the trucks were out of sight.

"We can get another receiver," he said.

"Where."

"There's a scavenger market at the Millford junction. Two days south."

"Two days south is four days round trip and we don't have four days."

"How do you know how many days we have?"

She was still holding the antenna. Eight sections of telescoping aluminium, each one thinner than the last, the whole thing collapsed to the length of her forearm. She turned it over in her hands the way Fen had turned over the receiver, looking for something, not sure what.

"I'll build another one," she said.

Tomás looked at her. "Out of what?"

She looked at the antenna. She looked at the scrubland on either side of the road, at the rusted signpost leaning into the ditch, at the wire that had once been a fence and was now just a suggestion of a fence running along the verge.

"Whatever I can find before dark," she said., -

The gas station had been gutted so thoroughly that even the thieves had given up on it. The pumps were gone, not just the nozzles but the housings, pulled out at the base and hauled away, leaving four concrete pedestals with ragged pipe stubs like broken teeth. The canopy still stood, one corner sagging where a support column had bent and never been straightened, and it threw a lopsided shadow across the forecourt in the late afternoon light. Inside the service bay, the lift pit was full of rainwater gone black with rust and old oil. The walls were spray-painted with overlapping tags, most of them from the first year after the Pulse when people still had paint and things to say.

Mara didn't care about any of that. She cared about the shelving unit still bolted to the back wall of the service bay, and the coil of copper wire she'd found under it, and the sheet metal she'd pried off a collapsed display rack, and the two screws she'd worked out of a junction box with the tip of her knife, and the length of insulated cable she'd stripped from the wall where someone had torn out the wiring but left the last three feet still stapled to the baseboard.

She laid it all out on the cleanest section of floor she could find, which was not very clean.

Tomás sat on an overturned milk crate near the bay door, watching her. He'd boiled water on the camp stove and handed her a cup without asking if she wanted one, which was one of the things she'd come to appreciate about him. The cup was sitting beside her left knee, still steaming.

She picked up the copper wire first. It was two-conductor, old enough that the insulation had gone stiff and cracked in places, but the copper itself was sound, she could see the bright metal where she'd stripped a test section. Twelve feet of it, maybe a little more.

She set it down and picked up the telescoping antenna.

Eight sections. The longest, fully extended, would give her roughly four feet. Not enough on its own. But the antenna wasn't the whole problem, the antenna was just the conductor. The problem was the feed point, the connection between the conductor and whatever she used for the receiver circuit, and the receiver circuit itself, which she didn't have because it was sitting in a livestock crate on an overpass with a padlock on it.

She stared at the components.

"You going to tell me what you're building," Tomás said, "or am I supposed to guess?"

"A wire aerial. Simple dipole if I can get the geometry right. Half-wave at the frequency I need."

"And the receiver part?"

"That's the harder problem."

She picked up the sheet metal, a strip about eight inches wide and fourteen long, bent slightly along one edge where she'd levered it free. She turned it over. The back surface was cleaner than the front, less oxidized. She set it down and picked up the insulated cable.

The cable had three conductors inside it. She'd need two of them for the aerial feed, and the third she could use for a ground. The junction box screws were steel, not brass, which wasn't ideal, but they were threaded and they were hers.

She started to strip the cable end.

"What was in the receiver that you can't replace?" Tomás asked.

"The tuning circuit. The filter." She worked the insulation back with her knife, careful not to nick the conductors. "A proper shortwave receiver has a bandpass filter, an IF stage, a detector. I can't build all of that from scratch. Not tonight."

"So what can you build?"

"A crystal set. Almost." She glanced up at him. "You know what a crystal set is?"

"Radio. First World War."

"Close enough. No power required. The signal drives the detector directly. The problem is sensitivity, a basic crystal set picks up strong local signals. What I'm looking for is buried in atmospheric static at a frequency that isn't broadcasting at high power." She paused. "But I have the antenna from the receiver. The tuning coil is still in it, Fen took the body but she didn't know the antenna has a loading coil in the base section." She held up the bottom section of the telescoping antenna, the thickest one, and shook it slightly. Something shifted inside with a faint, dense rattle. "She handed me the most important part and kept the casing."

Tomás was quiet for a moment. "She doesn't know that."

"No."

"So you can actually do this."

"I can build something. Whether it picks up the signal, " She set the antenna section down and reached for the copper wire. "I won't know until I try."

She began to measure the wire against her forearm, counting lengths. The frequency she needed was in the upper HF band, which meant a half-wave dipole would want roughly fifteen feet of conductor. She had twelve feet of copper wire. She had the antenna fully extended at four feet. If she could splice them cleanly at the feed point, she'd have sixteen feet of conductor, more than enough, and the loading coil in the antenna base would compensate for the mismatch.

She was doing the arithmetic in her head, which was where she did her best work. Numbers didn't lie to her. Numbers were the one thing in the wasteland that behaved the same way they always had.

"Mara."

She looked up.

Tomás had his elbows on his knees and was looking at her with the careful expression he used when he was about to say something he'd been holding for a while. "What does it say? The signal."

She kept her hands moving, stripping the copper wire, separating the conductors. "I told you. Structured transmission. Not noise."

"You told me what it is. I'm asking what it says."

The insulation came away in a clean spiral. She set the stripped section down and picked up the next length.

"Coordinates," she said.

"To what?"

"A location." She paused, deciding how much of this was true and how much was incomplete. "A bunker. Pre-collapse government facility. Retrofitted after the Pulse."

Tomás didn't say anything. She could hear him processing it, not the technical part, but the other part.

"How do you know it's real?" he said.

"The signal structure. It's layered, each transmission contains one coordinate layer, encoded in a way that requires the previous layer to decrypt. Whoever built it knew what they were doing. It's not a salvage beacon or a faction marker. It's a deliberate, structured contact protocol." She looked up. "Someone in that bunker is a professional."

"Or was."

"Or was," she agreed.

"And the location. Where is it?"

"Northwest. The second layer will give me the precise grid, but the first puts it somewhere in the high desert, past the Millford range." She kept her eyes on the wire. This was the true part. The incomplete part was what she hadn't decoded yet, the third transmission, the one she'd caught fragments of on three separate nights, the one that had a repeating numeric sequence she hadn't fully resolved but that had the structure of a countdown. She hadn't told him about that. Not because she'd decided not to. Because she hadn't decided yet.

That was what she told herself.

"A bunker," Tomás said. "With what in it?"

"I don't know yet."

He looked at her for a long moment. She kept her hands moving.

"You know something," he said. "You're not telling me all of it."

She set the wire down and looked at him directly. "I'm telling you what I've decoded. The second layer is what I need the receiver for, what I need *this*", she gestured at the components spread across the floor, "for. When I have the second layer, I'll know more."

It wasn't a lie. It was a careful arrangement of true things.

Tomás held her gaze for another moment, then nodded and looked away. He picked up his cup and drank. "All right," he said. "What do you need me to do?"

She felt something loosen slightly in her chest, not relief, not quite. Something more like the sensation of a wire under tension that had been given one more inch of slack.

"Find me something I can use as a ground stake," she said. "Metal rod, rebar, anything I can drive into the soil outside. And I need elevation, something I can run the aerial up to. Twelve feet minimum."

Tomás stood, stretching his back with a sound like a knuckle cracking. He looked around the service bay, then out at the forecourt. "The canopy support," he said. "The bent one. It's still bolted at the base. I can lash the aerial to it."

"That'll work."

He went out. She heard his boots on the concrete, then the sound of him testing the bent support column with his weight.

She turned back to the components.

The splice was the critical point, where the copper wire met the antenna's feed terminal, where the loading coil in the base section would do its work or fail to. She needed a clean electrical connection, not just twisted wire. She had no solder. She had the two steel screws from the junction box, and she had the sheet metal strip, and she had a length of time between now and dark that was shrinking.

She picked up the sheet metal and bent it carefully along the existing crease, working it back and forth until the metal fatigued and she had two pieces, each roughly four inches square. She drilled a hole in each piece with the tip of her knife, not a clean hole, a rough one, but a hole, and threaded a screw through each. Then she stripped the ends of both conductors she'd be connecting and wrapped them around the screws before tightening them down with the flat of the knife blade used as a makeshift driver.

It was ugly. It would work.

She was soldering the connection in her mind, the clean, bright bead of tin-lead alloy she'd have used before the Pulse, the smell of flux burning off, the satisfying solidity of a proper joint, when she stopped herself. That kind of thinking was a trap. You could spend your whole life mourning the tools you used to have, and meanwhile the thing in front of you didn't get built.

She tightened the second screw.

Tomás came back in with a length of rebar, still dirty from wherever he'd dug it. "Found this under the lift pit cover. There's about two feet of it."

"Perfect." She took it and set it aside. "The canopy support?"

"Solid enough. I can get the aerial up to about fourteen feet if I run it along the column and tie it off at the bend."

"Good." She began to lay out the full aerial run on the floor, the copper wire, the splice point, the antenna sections extended and locked. Sixteen feet, two inches. She looked at it for a moment, measuring it against the frequency in her head, running the arithmetic one more time.

"What are you calculating?" Tomás asked.

"Whether the length is right."

"Is it?"

"Close enough." She looked up. "Hand me that cable."

He handed her the three-conductor cable. She stripped the far end and separated the conductors, then connected two of them to the aerial feed point and the third to the rebar ground stake. The connection points were the sheet-metal clamps, both screws tight, both conductors wrapped and seated.

She held the completed assembly up and looked at it in the fading light from the bay door. It looked like junk. It looked like something a child had made from a pile of rubbish. The splice point was lumpy with wrapped wire. The sheet-metal clamps were rough-edged and slightly crooked. The rebar ground stake dangled from one end like a tail.

It was, as far as she could calculate, electrically correct.

"That's it?" Tomás said.

"That's the aerial. The detector is the loading coil in the antenna base, wired to the earpiece from my kit." She held up the small transducer she'd unclipped from her jacket pocket, a single earbud salvaged from a pre-collapse audio set, its cable stripped and re-terminated. "I listen through this. No amplification. I'll need the signal to be strong tonight, or I'll get nothing."

"What are the chances of that?"

She thought about the ionosphere, about how HF signals bounced off the F-layer at night and came in stronger and cleaner after dark, about how the bunker's transmitter, whatever it was, had been strong enough to reach her across two hundred miles of degraded atmosphere once before.

"Better than even," she said. "If they're transmitting tonight."

"And if they're not?"

She began to coil the aerial carefully, ready to run it up the canopy support. "Then we wait for the next transmission window and I try again."

She didn't say what happened if there was no next window. She didn't say what happened if the countdown she hadn't decoded yet was already running.

Outside, the sun had dropped behind the scrubland and the sky was going the colour of a bruise, deep purple at the horizon, fading up through grey. The first stars were coming out, faint and cold. Somewhere to the north, a coyote called once and went quiet.

Tomás held the bay door open for her as she carried the aerial out to the forecourt.

"For what it's worth," he said, "I think it's real."

She looked at him.

"The bunker," he said. "I think it's real. I've been trying to decide since you told me, and that's where I landed."

She didn't know what to do with that, the plainness of it, the way he'd said *I've been trying to decide* as if it were a simple thing to say. She turned back to the canopy support and began to lash the aerial to it with a length of paracord.

"Help me get this up," she said.

He came and held the column steady while she climbed two feet up the base and tied off the first section of aerial. The metal was cold under her hands. Above them, the bent canopy creaked once in a wind she couldn't feel at ground level.

Fourteen feet up, the copper wire caught the last of the light and held it for a moment before the sky went dark., -

The signal came in at 0214.

She'd been sitting cross-legged on the forecourt for four hours with the earbud pressed against her ear and the aerial lead running up the canopy column above her, and she'd heard nothing but the low, continuous hiss of atmospheric static, the ocean sound, she'd always called it, the white noise of the ionosphere doing its work. Tomás had slept two hours in the garage and come back out at midnight with a strip of dried meat and a canteen, sat down beside her without speaking, and gone on watching the dark.

Then the pattern came through the static like a hand tapping on the other side of a wall.

She pressed the earbud in harder and closed her eyes. The signal was faint, she had to hold completely still to separate it from the background hiss, but it was there, and it was structured. She pulled the small notebook from her jacket and began transcribing by touch, writing in the dark, the pencil moving on muscle memory alone.

Tomás watched her hand move and said nothing.

It took eleven minutes. When the transmission ended she opened her eyes and looked at what she'd written, tilting the notebook toward the faint grey of the sky.

The second coordinate layer resolved in twenty minutes of work, the pencil moving and stopping and moving again, the notebook filling with numbers and crossed-out numbers and circled numbers. She was aware of Tomás watching, aware of the cold coming up through the concrete under her, aware of nothing else.

When she had it, she sat still for a moment.

"How far?" Tomás said.

She hadn't spoken aloud. He'd read it off her face.

"The partial grid put the bunker at roughly two-twenty miles southwest." She looked at the notebook. "The second layer corrects that. It's forty miles further. Two-sixty, and it's not southwest, it's west-southwest." She paused. "That puts it inside Crale's core territory. Not the edge. The interior."

Tomás was quiet for a moment. Then: "How far inside?"

"Far enough that we'd be crossing three of his supply corridors to reach it."

He looked at the aerial above them, then at the notebook. "You said the signal had a third layer."

"Yes."

"Did you get it tonight?"

She had. The third layer had come in the final burst of the transmission, a time-indexed sequence she'd recognised immediately, the encoding pattern clean and deliberate. She worked it out now, on the next page of the notebook, while Tomás waited. The pencil moved in tight shorthand, crossing and circling, arriving at a number she checked twice before she looked up.

Eleven.

She showed him the page.

"Days?" he said.

"Days. The bunker's backup power fails in eleven days. After that, the transmission stops. The ventilation stops." She didn't need to say what else stopped. "Whoever is in there, they've been running on stored power for seven years. They're at the end of it."

Tomás looked at the number for a long time. Then he picked up the canteen and drank. "We need to move at first light."

"Yes."

"And Fen?"

She looked at the aerial, the improvised, ugly, electrically-correct aerial that bore no resemblance to the clean receiver Fen's people had stripped from her pack. "She said she'd look at us again in the morning.", -

Fen came at dawn with two of her people, both armed, both quiet. She walked a slow circuit around the aerial assembly on the canopy column, studying it from different angles, her hands in her jacket pockets.

Mara stood beside the garage bay and watched her look.

The aerial was copper wire, rebar, sheet-metal clamps, and paracord. It was a field antenna. It was not a receiver, not a transmitter, not any kind of communication device by any reasonable definition. It received nothing without a detector and an earpiece, and the earpiece was in Mara's pocket and had been there all night, and Fen had not confiscated earpieces.

Fen completed her circuit and looked at Mara. "What does it do?"

"Picks up atmospheric noise." Mara kept her voice flat. "I'm mapping static patterns. Background research."

Fen looked at the aerial again. One of her people, a young man with a rifle slung barrel-down, crouched and examined the rebar ground stake, turning it over, finding nothing interesting.

"Background research," Fen said.

"That's right."

A long pause. Somewhere behind the scrub line a bird was making a sound like a hinge in need of oil. The sky was pale and cold, the sun not yet above the horizon, and the forecourt smelled of old rubber and the faint mineral sharpness of dew on concrete.

"All right," Fen said. She turned and walked back toward the road without looking at either of them again. Her two people followed.

Mara waited until they were past the fuel pump before she let out a breath.

Tomás came out of the garage with both packs. He handed hers over without comment. She broke down the aerial in four minutes, unscrewing the clamps, coiling the copper wire, pulling the rebar from the ground, and packed it into the bottom of her bag under the notebook and the coil of spare cable. The sheet-metal clamps she left on the forecourt. They were too heavy to carry and she could make more.

They were moving by the time the sun cleared the scrub., -

The fastest route on Tomás's hand-marked map ran southwest along what had been a state highway before the Pulse, and for the first six miles it was open ground, cracked asphalt, scrub pushing up through the median, the occasional stripped car chassis sitting at an angle where it had rolled off the shoulder seven years ago and never been moved. They walked in the shade of the tree line where there was one, in the open where there wasn't, and Mara kept the notebook in her jacket pocket and thought about the number eleven.

Eleven days. She calculated it three different ways as she walked and arrived at the same answer each time. If they maintained their current pace, twenty miles a day on good ground, less on bad, they could reach the corrected coordinates in twelve days. One day too long.

They needed to cut a day. That meant no rest stops longer than necessary, no detours for safety that weren't strictly unavoidable, and the fastest route at every choice point.

She looked at the map over Tomás's shoulder at the four-mile mark when they stopped to drink.

The fastest route to the southwest, past the six-mile mark, ran through a section of collapsed overpass. The highway had passed under a rail bridge at this point, and the bridge had come down, partially, the map notation said, in Tomás's small, careful handwriting, sometime in the first year after the Pulse. The notation said: *passable, low clearance, check before committing.*

"How low?" she asked.

Tomás looked at the map. "Last time I came through it was about four feet at the lowest point. Maybe two hundred metres of it."

"When was last time?"

"Eight months ago."

She looked at the notation. *Check before committing.* "Is there another route?"

"Three miles east and then south. Adds four hours."

She did the arithmetic. Four hours today, four hours they didn't have. "We go through."

Tomás folded the map. He said nothing., -

They reached the underpass at midmorning.

The rail bridge had come down at an angle, the eastern end dropping further than the western, so the approach from the north showed a dark mouth of compressed space, the original highway clearance crushed to roughly half its height, the concrete overhead fractured into hanging slabs held in place by their own weight and the rebar threading through them. The road surface inside was buried under a foot of grey dust and debris. At the edges, where the bridge deck had ground against the highway walls, the concrete had crumbled into loose rubble that had spilled across the lanes and been compressed by whatever foot traffic had passed through since.

Mara stopped at the entrance and looked in. The far end was visible, a pale rectangle of daylight two hundred metres away, slightly brighter on the left side where the collapse was less complete. The tunnel was dark in the middle, the overhead slabs blocking the sky, and the air coming out of it was cold and tasted of concrete dust and something older, something sealed.

She turned to say something to Tomás and stopped.

He was standing six feet back from the entrance. His pack was on his back and his hands were at his sides and he was looking at the dark mouth of the underpass with the fixed, careful expression of a man who was doing something very difficult with his face.

His breathing was audible. Not fast, controlled, deliberate, each breath drawn in and let out at the same measured pace. The kind of breathing that was work.

Mara turned back to the entrance.

She crouched and looked at the overhead slabs. She moved her gaze along the ceiling from the entrance inward, section by section, the way she'd have scanned a circuit board for a fault. The first twenty metres looked stable, the slabs were large and the fracture lines ran parallel to the road rather than across it, which meant they were less likely to drop in chunks. The middle section, where the light failed, she couldn't assess from here. The far section was lit well enough to read.

"The first twenty metres are solid," she said, not turning around. "The fracture pattern runs longitudinal. That's what you want, it means the load is distributing along the length rather than concentrating at the break points." She stood and moved to the left edge of the entrance, where the original lane marking was still faintly visible under the dust. "The safest line is left of centre. The right side has loose rubble from the wall collapse, you'd be walking on unstable material. Left side, the debris has been compacted by foot traffic. Firmer footing."

She heard him come up behind her. Not close, still a few feet back, but moving.

"The low point will be somewhere in the middle section," she said. "Probably around the hundred-metre mark based on the angle of the drop. That's where we'll need to crouch. I'd estimate three and a half feet of clearance at the minimum, which means hands and knees for about ten metres, then it opens back up." She pulled her flashlight from her pack, a small hand-crank unit, pre-collapse, the lens slightly yellowed, and wound it six turns. The beam came on, pale but steady. "I'll go first and call the clearance as I go. You follow my voice."

She didn't look at him.

She stepped into the underpass.

The cold came up immediately, the trapped cold of enclosed concrete, the kind that didn't cycle with the day. The dust under her boots was fine and deep and each step raised a small silent cloud that drifted in the flashlight beam. Above her, the fractured slabs were closer than they'd looked from outside, close enough that she could see the individual aggregate in the concrete, the small stones and sand that had been mixed in before the pour, now exposed along the break lines.

"Ceiling is stable," she called back. Her voice came back at her from the walls, slightly flattened. "First section clear. Left of centre, watch the right edge."

She heard him enter behind her. His boots in the dust. The sound of his breathing, still measured, still deliberate.

She kept moving. She called the ceiling height as she went, not because it was necessary, not because he couldn't see for himself, but because her voice was something to follow and she knew it and he knew it and neither of them was going to say so.

"Ceiling dropping. Still three feet minimum. You'll want to duck in about five more steps."

The light from the entrance was gone behind her now. The pale rectangle ahead was the only reference point, and it was still a hundred metres away. The flashlight beam picked out the overhead slabs in close-up detail, the rebar ends protruding from the broken edges, the dark staining where water had come through in the first years and then stopped. The dust had a smell here, deep in the middle section, a dry mineral smell with something underneath it she couldn't identify. Old exhaust, maybe, trapped in the concrete for seven years.

"Low point. Hands and knees."

She went down without ceremony and crawled. The dust was cold under her palms and the pack shifted forward on her back and she had to keep her head turned sideways to keep the flashlight aimed ahead. The concrete overhead was eighteen inches from her face. She could see every crack.

She kept talking. "Floor is solid here. Rebar on the right side, two o'clock, don't put your hand on it. The clearance is opening back up. Another eight metres."

Behind her, his breathing. Still controlled. Still working.

"Five metres."

She felt the ceiling rise before she measured it, the cold air moved differently, the acoustic quality of the space changed, the flashlight beam reached further before it hit the overhead slabs. She came up out of the crawl and stood in a crouch, then straightened to her full height.

"Clear. Standing room. Thirty metres to the exit."

She heard him come up out of the crawl behind her. The sound of his pack settling as he stood. One breath, in, out, that was slightly less controlled than the others.

She walked toward the exit and didn't look back.

The pale rectangle of daylight grew and brightened, and then she stepped out into the open air and the sun hit her face and the smell of concrete dust gave way to dry grass and distance and the faint resin smell of scrub pine.

She stood in the sunlight and looked at the map. She heard Tomás come out behind her. She heard him stop. She heard him breathe, two, three breaths, the kind that were just breathing, not work.

She studied the map.

After a moment he came and stood beside her. "Southwest from here," he said. His voice was level.

"Southwest," she agreed. She folded the map and put it away. "We've got good ground for the next four miles."

They started walking.

The underpass was behind them. Neither of them looked back at it, and neither of them said anything about it, and the silence between them was the comfortable kind, the kind that had been earned, as they moved out into the open land with eleven days left and forty miles more of Crale's territory ahead of them than either of them had planned for., -

The ground levelled out three hours past the underpass, long flat miles of scrub and cracked asphalt where a state highway had been, the centre line still faintly visible in places, bleached to a ghost by seven years of sun. They made good time. Mara used it.

She kept the notebook out as she walked, cross-referencing the coordinates from the overnight decode against the map. The numbers were right, she'd checked them twice in the dark and once in the dawn light before Fen arrived, but she ran them again anyway, because the forty-mile correction changed everything about the route and she needed to know the changed picture precisely, not approximately.

The numbers kept coming out the same.

She stopped walking.

Tomás went two steps further before he noticed. He turned. "Problem?"

"Give me a minute."

She sat down on a chunk of broken kerb at the road's edge, concrete worn smooth on top, a dandelion growing in the crack beside it, yellow and precise, and opened the notebook across her knees. She looked at the corrected coordinates. She looked at the map. She put her finger on the spot.

Tomás came back and crouched beside her, forearms on his knees, not touching the notebook. He waited.

"The second layer is a refinement," she said. "The first coordinate set I decoded, the partial grid, that was a broadcast position. General area. Wide enough to reach anyone with the right equipment within a few hundred miles." She tapped the notebook. "The precise location is forty miles deeper. A different encoding system, you'd need both layers to get the real coordinates, which I think was deliberate. In case the signal was intercepted."

"Smart."

"Yes." She turned the notebook so he could see the numbers. "The bunker isn't at the partial-grid location. It's here." She put her finger on the map. The spot was well past the line she'd drawn two days ago, the line that marked the edge of the territory where Tomás's knowledge of the roads ran thin and Crale's patrols ran thick. Her finger was forty miles past that line.

Tomás looked at where her finger was. He looked at it for a long time. Then he straightened up and stood with his back to her, looking out at the flat scrub, and she could see the calculation going on in the set of his shoulders, not panic, not refusal, just the working-through of a man who had learned to price things accurately.

She waited.

He turned back. "The rate we agreed was for the partial-grid location."

"I know."

"That territory, " he nodded toward the southwest, toward the invisible forty miles, "I've been through it twice. Once alone, once with a group of five. The second time we lost one of the five at a patrol crossing near the old county road junction. Crale's people don't run checkpoints that far in. They run sweeps. Different problem. Harder to read, harder to talk your way through."

"I know."

He named a figure. It was in ammunition, thirty rounds of .308, which was what he used, which was what she'd been carrying as trade weight since the settlement. Thirty rounds was most of what she had.

She didn't haggle.

She said, "Yes."

He looked at her. Something shifted in his expression, not surprise exactly, but a recalibration, the way a man adjusts when the evidence changes the picture. He'd been watching her bargain for two days. He knew what her not bargaining meant.

"All right," he said. He looked at the map again. "We camp two hours before dark, not one. I want to be off the road before the light changes. Crale's sweeps use the dusk window."

"Understood."

"And we go quiet from here. No fires after the first night. No signals you don't have to send."

She nodded. She closed the notebook and put it away. She adjusted the antenna lashed to her pack, tightened the wire connection at the feed point, which had been working loose on the rough ground, and stood.

They started walking.

The road ran southwest ahead of them, straight and empty, the broken centre line disappearing into the distance like a sentence that had been interrupted mid-word., -

They made camp in the hollow of a dry creek bed two hours before dark, as Tomás had said. The banks cut the wind and hid the firelight, and he fed the fire with sticks no thicker than his thumb so it burned hot and low and left almost no smoke. Around them the scrub had gone dark and dimensionless, the sky overhead hard with stars. Somewhere out in the flat a nighthawk called once and was not answered.

Mara sat with the notebook balanced on her knee and the earbud in, the rebuilt aerial, copper wire and the loading coil from the confiscated receiver's antenna, wired to the earpiece from her kit, propped against the creek bank at the angle she'd calculated would give her the best sky-path to the southwest. She'd been listening for forty minutes. Static. The ocean sound.

Then the pattern came through.

She pressed the earbud in harder and closed her eyes. The signal was clean, cleaner than the night before, the ionosphere doing its work now that the temperature had dropped and the F-layer had lifted. She transcribed by touch, the pencil moving in the dark on muscle memory alone.

Tomás watched her hand move and said nothing.

It took nine minutes. When it ended she opened her eyes and looked at what she'd written by the firelight.

The third layer. She'd been waiting for it, the time-indexed sequence she'd seen the shape of in the overnight decode, the one she hadn't had enough of to resolve until now. She worked it out on the next page, the pencil moving in tight shorthand, crossing and circling. The encoding was the same system as the second layer, which meant she had the key already. The arithmetic was fast.

She looked at the number.

She looked at it for a long time.

Eleven days from the first transmission she'd received. That had been two days ago.

Nine days.

The fire popped. A stick collapsed into coals, and the light shifted, and for a moment her shadow stretched long across the creek bank and then contracted again. She was aware of Tomás across the fire, eating methodically, watching the dark in the slow patient way he had, the scan of a man who treated stillness as information.

She turned to a fresh page in the notebook and wrote the number in her shorthand. The notation looked like a frequency reading, like a signal-strength log. If someone found the notebook and didn't know the system, they would find calibration data. She closed it.

"Anything?" Tomás said. He was still looking out at the dark.

"Third layer's decoded."

"And?"

"Confirms the countdown." She paused. "Nine days now."

He nodded once, the way he acknowledged things he'd already factored in. He set his tin cup down on the flat stone beside the fire and reached into his pack for the binoculars, a pre-collapse pair, the rubber eyecups cracked and repaired with electrical tape, but the optics still sharp. He stood, moved to the top of the creek bank, and lay flat against the rim.

She watched him scan.

The binoculars swept east, back along the road they'd come in on. He held them steady for a moment, then moved them slightly, held again. The nighthawk called a second time, from a different direction, and this time something answered it, or something made a sound that could have been an answer if you weren't paying attention.

Tomás stayed still.

Then he came back down the bank in a controlled slide, moving quietly, and crouched beside her. He didn't hand her the binoculars. He kept them in his hands, turned them over once, set them down.

"Dust signature," he said. "East. Maybe eight miles."

She felt something go cold in her chest.

"Moving?"

"Was. It's settled now, they've made camp. But the signature's wrong for wind. Too concentrated, too low. That's road dust from vehicles or a group moving in formation." He picked up the binoculars again, turned them in his hands without looking through them, a habit she'd noticed, he handled things when he was thinking. "They weren't there an hour ago."

"How many?"

"Can't say. The dust says at least four, maybe six. Moving fast before they stopped." He looked at her. "Fast and in formation. That's not scavengers. Scavengers spread out."

She thought about the checkpoint two days back. The man with the radio, the deliberate way he'd noted their direction of travel, the pause before he'd waved them through. She'd told herself it was standard. She'd told herself the receiver's confiscation and return was the end of it.

She'd been wrong about that.

"Sable," she said.

Tomás didn't ask who that was. He'd heard the name at the settlement, the same as she had, Crale's advance unit, the lieutenant who moved ahead of the main force the way a hand moves ahead of a body reaching for something. "Maybe," he said. "Probably."

She looked east into the dark, though there was nothing to see. Eight miles. At the pace a formation moved on open road, that was a day's march. One day behind them.

She opened the notebook again. She looked at the nine-day number she'd written in shorthand at the top of the page. She looked at the forty miles between their current position and the bunker. She did the arithmetic.

Nine days. Forty miles into Crale's territory, where his people ran sweeps instead of checkpoints, where the roads thinned and the sight lines opened and there was nowhere to talk your way through anything. At the pace they'd been making, fifteen miles a day on good ground, less on bad, that was three days of travel, maybe four if the terrain was what Tomás said it was.

Which left five days of margin.

Which was not a margin. A margin was something you could afford to lose. Five days was a number that looked like a margin until you factored in the sweep patterns, the terrain, the rebuilt antenna that was already working loose again, the fact that she still had to stay ahead of whatever was moving behind them.

And one day behind them, a unit that moved fast and in formation.

She closed the notebook.

"We leave before first light," she said.

"Yes."

"How far to the county road junction? The one where you lost the man from your group."

He was quiet for a moment. "Day and a half. Maybe less if we push the morning hours."

"We push them."

He nodded. He picked up the binoculars one more time, looked east, put them away. Then he began breaking down the fire, not stamping it, which threw sparks, but smothering it with a flat stone, pressing down until the last coal went dark and the creek bed filled with the smell of killed smoke and cooling earth.

She sat in the sudden dark and let her eyes adjust.

Eleven days from the first signal. Nine remaining. One day's lead over whatever was moving behind them. Forty miles of Crale's territory between her and a door that would seal itself shut the moment the power ran out.

She thought about the seed vault. She thought about what it meant, not abstractly, not as a concept, but concretely: grain that would grow, varieties that had been preserved against exactly this kind of catastrophe, a biological library that could restart what the Pulse had ended. She thought about the people at the settlement eating the same three crops in rotation because those were the only seeds that had survived in any quantity, and the slow arithmetic of that, the narrowing, year by year, of what the land could offer.

She thought about what it would mean for Crale to control it.

She stood. She adjusted the antenna on her pack, tightened the wire at the feed point, tested the connection with her thumb. It held.

Above her, the stars were hard and indifferent, the same stars that had been there before the Pulse and would be there long after every calculation she was making had resolved one way or the other.

She shouldered the pack.

Nine days. One day's lead. Forty miles.

She began to think about what it would take to make that enough.
